title: 5 Ways To Respond To Wrong Answers
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the tension between the need to give students honest, useful feedback and the desire to keep them comfortable enough to keep sharing. He offers five specific phrases for responding to an incorrect or off-target answer without embarrassing, rejecting, or discouraging the student: asking how they arrived at their answer to let them self-correct; affirming they're "on the right track, but not there yet"; expressing genuine interest in an unexpected but valid interpretation; offering a hint when a student is far off course; and simply saying "thank you" while working through a full round of volunteers before revealing the correct answer. Each technique is paired with an explanation of when it works best and why it preserves both accuracy and student confidence. Linsin frames the overall goal as being a "straight but compassionate shooter" — giving students the honest feedback they need to grow intellectually while protecting the psychological safety that keeps them willing to take risks.
points: Students need honest, direct feedback to grow intellectually, but that feedback must be delivered without embarrassment or rejection.
"How did you arrive at your answer?" lets students self-correct by walking back through their own reasoning.
"You're on the right track, but not there yet" validates thinking while still signaling more work is needed.
For students far off course, offering a hint keeps them productively wrestling toward the answer rather than being told outright.
Thanking every volunteer before revealing the correct answer lets more students participate and self-correct without public judgment.
quotes: There are those who believe you should never tell a student who volunteers an answer that they’re wrong.

The five responses above are proven ways to give genuine feedback without discouraging your students or throwing a wet blanket over good discussion.
